Information has reached this Island from St. Thomas of a Mutiny having been committed on the high seas by the crew of an American vessel, and of the þÿMutineers arrival at that port. Unlike other places, we have invariably found it a difficult matter to he furnished witli authentic particulars of any oc- ; drowned the currence, whether of moment or trivial, ami m placing before our readers a few outlines of t tins case, we do so merely upon t.ie autnonty of what we have heard related. It appca.s that an American brigantine (her in. me we have not heard), with a ei ew of lour Portuguese ; and two Englishmen, besides tiie Cook, Mato and Captain, had sailed from the port of New York, with an assorted cargo, bound to tho ; coast of Africa, on a trading voyage, and alter being at sea some days it was found that gieat I dissatisfaction prevailed among the crew. Oil I U. S. Frigate þÿ
was suddenly struck a blow by one of the men | Welch it was with a þÿ þÿheaver, upon which he cried for help. The mate and cook were both in the cabin at
to the spot, wlieu a knile was plunged into the body of the latter, killing him on the spot.

The mate seeing this, retreated to await his doom, but Providence directed that his life should be spared. While this scene was being enacted the captain was struck a second blow, and in the .act of imploring mercy, the same assassin who had just imbued his hands in the þÿcook b s lood, made far the captain and lodged the bloody knife into his body. The dead bodies were then thrown overboard, and a consultation was held as to the disposal of the mate. The mind may easily picture to itself what must have been his feelings when he was summoned into the presence of these men As fate would have it, the mate happened to be the only navigator left on board, and the mutineers fearing that they would be risking their own lives had they killed him, consented to spare his life upon condition that lie would enter upon the log-book what they would dictate, and after that steer them into some port of safety. This he naturally consented to do þÿ and what means, we would ask, will a man not resort to to save his own life þÿ .aid wrote to the effect that both captain and cook had died on certain dates from sickness, the mate pledging himself never to disclose the awful tragedy. It was then resolved that the vessel should put into St. Thomas some say by the stratagem of the mate, on the plea of getting a supply of water. After arriving there the mate immediately went ashore and reported the matter to the authorities, who promptly had the crew arrested and lodged in prison, to be hereafter dealt with. We learn

that the men do not deny the murderous act, but plead the former cruelty of the captain to w irds them in justification of the atrocious deed. It is also stated that the two Englishmen took no part in the murder, but being at the mercy of the other men offered no opposition. The deceased þÿcaptain s name was Lassen (a Dane), and the name of the mate, through whose instrumen ality these men have been brought to justice, is PBTRiGUS, also a Dane. No doubt by the return of the schooners from St Thomas we may be placed in possession of fuller particulars relative to this matter

The following is, according to advices received from Denmark, the outline of the treaty about to be concluded between Denmark and the various European Powers trading with the Baltic, for the redemption of the sound dues: The preamble states that, with a view to facilitate and increase the Commercial and Maritime relations at present existing between Denmark and the other contracting States, these parties have agreed to negotiate a treaty for abolishing the dues levied on ships and their cargoes passing through the Sound and the Belts, and for diminishing the transit duty payable on goods passing overland from the Baltic. In the 1st Article the King of Denmark undertakes for the future not to levy any duty tonnage, or for lighthouses, buoys, &c , on any vessels or their cargoes, passing from the German Ocean to the Baltic, or vice versa through the Belts or the Sound, and this, too, irrespective of whether the vessels simply pass through the Danish waters, or whether they be compelled by stress of weather or for the sake of commercial operations to cast anchor there, or to put into a port. No vessel of any sort belonging to the contracting Powers, is in future to be subjected to detention or other hindrance while passing through the Belts or the Sound. In the 2nd article the King binds himself to maintain and keep in good order all the lights, beacons, buoys, &c., at present in use, both at the approaches to Danish ports and roads, or along the Danish coast. Secondly, in the interest of Commerce and Navigation, to pay due regard to the expediency of modifying the position, or the form of these said lights, bea-

ber, and this without any charge or burden to foreign vessels. Thirdly, to keep up the present supply of Pilots, whom it shall be optional to question of the Principalities is to be made an all Masters of vessels to employ or not. The charges for Pilotage are also never to rise higher than they are at present ; they are to be the same for Danish as for foreign vessels, and are to he payable only by those vessels that take Pilots on board. Fourthly, he will permit private individuals, whether natives or foreigners, to establish stations in the Sound and Belts for providing steam-tugs to vessels

passing through and desirous of profitting by this facility. Fifthly, he extends to all canals or other routes leading from the German Ocean to the Baltic the same exemption from duty which Danish and foreign merchandise of certain kinds enjoy on certain routes (here follows a specification of the various kinds of merchandise and the various routes) ; and if in future any goods not specified here should succeed in obtaining an exemption from transit duty on any one of these routes, that cxenip tion shall be extended to nil others. And sixthly, he undertakes to reduce the rate of transit duty on all those goods now liable to it to an uniform rate of 10 skillings Banish money, for 500lb. Danish weight ! and finally, should the transit dues come, at any future time, to be lowered on any one of the routes below this rate, the King undertakes to put all the routes now connecting, or which may hereafter connect, the German Ocean or the Elbe with the Baltic or any of its tributaries, on a footing of perfect equlity with any routes that may hereafter be opened between any two ports of his dominions According to Art. 3, the provisions of Articles 1 and 2 are to come into force on and after April the 1st of this year. Art. 4, binds the States entering into this treaty with Denmark to pay the latter as an indemnification for the sacrifices it makes in the above articles the sum of 30,570,698 rixdollars, according to various quotas already agreed upon, and with the provision that each

State is liable only for its own quota. In Art. 5 it is provided that the various amounts above specified shall be paid within þÿ 20 years, in 40 half-yearly equal instalments, which shall include the portion of the capital due and the interest that accrues on the outstanding balance. Each of the high contracting parties undertakes in Article 6 to come to an agreement with the King of Denmark as to þÿ 1, the manner how, and the place where, these half-yearly payments shall be made ; 2, the manner and the rate in which the several amounts, as stated in Danish money, shall be computed in the money of the said State ; and 3, the conditions and the manner in which the said State reserves to itself (if at all) to pay off by anticipation its quota of the indemnity money. In the following and concluding article the execution of the foregoing stipulations is made to be dependent on the accomplishment of the formalities required by the constitutional laws of the high contracting States, who however, undertake to procure that sanction at the ear liest possible time.
From the Illustrated London News, Felt. 14.j THE UNION OF THE PRINCJ PA LITIES-

It was reported at Constantinople on the 29th that the Moldo-Wallachian Divans would propose the union of the two Principalities into one, by a considerable majority. It was also said that the Porte would altogether relinquish its resistance to the scheme, and content itself with stipulating that no foreign Prince should become the Sovereign of the new State. The article in the Moniteur of the 4th relative to the future organisation of the Danubian Principalities, has produced a very unpleasant impression at Vienna. The Vienne Presse observes, that the recent policy of France in the Eastern question cannot excite astonishment if it is considered that Count Moray is to pass the winter at St. Petersburg, and the Grand Duke Constantine to visit the Emperor Napoleon in the spring. The most remarkable passage in the article in question is the followþÿing: The mask has now been laid aside, and the

affair of the highest importance. The declaration of the Moniteur will give fresh vigour and courage to Russia, for the union of the Danubian Principalities will he the first great step towards the breaking up of Turkey þÿ it will be a positive encroachment on the sovereign rights of the Sultan, and an act of hostility towards the Powers which closed up the land and sea routes from Russia to Constantinople.

(From the þÿ Loudon Times, February 13 ) þÿ The satisfactory settlement of the questions relating to the Danubiau Principalities cannot but bo endangered by such an imprudent manifesto as appeared a few days since in the Monitmr. AVe should be willing to believe that to haste, or thoughtlessness, or the indiscretion of some official personage, was duo the publication of this very indiscreet article; but the appearance of similar arguments in other journals which commonly represent the opinions of the French Government leaves no doubt that the Imperial Cabinet not only desires the union of the Principalities, but thinks fit to announce its wishes for the purpose of influencing the deliberations of the Moldo- Wallaehians themselves. The result of such a step might have been expected. Lord Clarendon, in answer to Lord Lyndhurst on Monday night, did not hesitate to say that he had read the article in the Monitcur with surprise, since at the time of the Congress of Paris an understanding had been come to by the representatives of the Great Powers that, until the Divans had met, until the Commissioners had made their report, and the Congress had assembled to consider it, no ono of the Powers would do anything to influence opinion in the Principalities or elsewhere on this question. An avowedly official article, proclaiming the desire of the French Government to unito the provinces, its intention to impress its wishes on the other Powers, and its hope of gaining for its views a majority in the Confe-

rences which are to come, is certainly as plain a breach of the former understanding as can well be conceived. So the representatives of Austria and Turkey, as well as Lord Clarendon, seem to have thought, and it is said that explanations have been asked respecting the sudden and peremptory manifesto of the French Government. While the several Cabiuets are corresponding on the subject we may take the opportunity ouce more to call attention to the state of the regions which, through the immediate cause of the late war, have now been almost forgotten by all but professed politicians. The pretext with which Russia covered her designs of aggrandisement used to he, as we all know, the deliverance of the oppressed Christians from Mussulman thraldom. By this the Czar induced Europe to acquiesce iu his protectorate of the Principalities. Four years ago the most lar-secing politician would have confessed that, iu his opinion, Moldavia and Wallachia must, before many years, be brought under the direct dominion of Russia. The Russians had crossed the Pruth whenever they chose, and remained as long as seemed good to them. The native authorities had been suspended or superseded at the pleasure of the protectors, and any person hostile to the Russian supremacy had been speedily driven from the country. In fact, the late Czar looked upon the country as virtually his own, and in the summer of 1853 thought that the time had come to convert an actual into a legal sovereignty. How nearly this arrogant

confidence was justified by the result we well know. Now that Russia has been defeated iu a great war people may be inclined to under-estimate the danger which Europe escaped, but a little reflection on the events of 1853 will convince them that hut for the firmness of the AVestcrn Powers, aided by a concurrence of circumstances which may not again take place, the Russians might have made themselves masters of one of the finest tracts of Europe, containing 5,000,000 of people, commanding the Danube during the greater part of its navigable course, and overlapping the eastern provinces of Austria, so as to bring that empire into a state of completo military dependence. To prevent such a catastrophe England and France went to war and Austria occupied the disputed provinces. Evidently the object of Europe now must he to prevent the recurrence of such an invasion. How, then, shall it bo prevented ? Surely, by the means that were found successful on the last occasion. In 1854 the Russians retired because a Turkish army was in their front, the Austrians on their flank, and the French and English ready to march to reinforco these two armies. Any scheme for the settlement of the Principalities must, therefore, be such as will not prevent the free military action of the Porte in the country, and the right of the Sultan to call in the aid of tho three great Powers which arc interested in his support. Now, the wish of Russia naturally is to weaken the connexion between Turkey and thoso outlying
provinces. Russia cares nothing about the Rouman nation, and in the old times, when she

T c R 0 I X A; V/ lj , looked upon the whole country as a sure prize, any patriot who should have suggested the union of the Principalities would soon have had to fly across the Danube. But now her game is to detach them from Turkey by establishing a spurious independence. The provinces are governed separately by Hospodars, who, under a proper system, might be appointed by the Porte with every security for the good government of \ the people, The Czar, however, is not content with this, and demands that the national feeling of the Roumaus shall be gratified by the union of the two provinces, which will thus, it is urged, receive a surer guarantee for their liberties. In fact, a Roumau State is to be erected somewhat on the model of the Greek kingdom. Nothing is said about the position of the ruler, but there can be little doubt that the next step would be to substitute an hereditary Sovereign for the nominee of the Porte. It will be remembered that Greece began with a President, hut was soon changed into a Monarchy, which has become, as far as the will of the Court is concerned, a mere dependency of'Russia. Now, such a result in tho case of the Moldo-Walluchian territory England is surely bound to guard against. Who can doubt the consequences of establishing on the banks of the Danube a State tending to become every day more and more independent of Constantinople? The people of the provinces have no claim he be considered as a separate nation. They belong to a race of which several millions inhabit Austrian territory, and a large

number tho Russian province of Bessarabia. If there is to be a Routnan nation, the Czar should give up part of his own dominions to the Government at Bucharest ; if, as is no doubt the case, the new State is to be merely a tool of Russia, we can see nothing but danger to Turkey and embarrassment to Europe in the intrigues to which its existence would give rise. Nor are the Moldo-AVallachians fitted by position or capacity to play an independent part in Europe. Their country is a perfect plain, and naturally indefensible. They themselves are of the stuff which may well be built iuto the fabric of other empires, but has not the hardness and solidity to stand by itself. A small body of Boyards, luxurious without taste or iutelligencc, apiug Paris and its doings iu their provincial way, and caring nothing for their own nation or any other as long as they can obtain the means of living in idleness and indulgence ; au army of priests, poor and uneducated, all at the service of Russia, and looking up to the Czar with religious reverence; and, finally, a sort peasantry, which it seems a mockery to call upon to deliberate in the forthcoming Divans þÿ a class without the elements of instruction, and without hope or care for any change in their degraded lot þÿ such are the elements of which Moldo-AVallachian society is composed. Who can for a moment be deluded by the commonplaces uttered respecting liberty and nationality, or believe that this corrupt and unlettered population can be any-

thing else than the instrument of the powerful Monarchy, the aggressive spirit of which is not likely to be tamed by a single defeat ? We regret, therefore, that the French Government should have a second time allowed itself to he influenced by the representations which Russia, in accordance with her natural policy, has not ceased to make. The endeavours of our late enemy to gain over the French Court and people are sufficiently notorious, but they have been marked with so little tact and have been so obvious in their purpose that we can hardly account for their success with a people so quickwitted and sensitive to the ludicrous. However, perseverance has had its reward, and in tho French press and French society Russian opinions have lately found a sufficiently favourable reception. But we cannot doubt that the good sense of the Emperor will cause him to take a clear view of this important question In spite of articles official or semi-official we believe that the course which justice and sound policy deinuid must eventually receive the assent ot the Tuileries. If tho allies permit so great an invasion of tho þÿSultan rights s as is involved in the union of tho Principalities, it may be predicted that the war will prove to have been waged iu vain. The interests of Europe demand that tho status of these provinces during centuries shall be still preserved, and that no political experiment shall bo tried on so valuable a subject. It will, we think, be the duty of England to de-
clare positively against any tampering with the integrity of the Turkish empire, and to act with firmness iu support of the resolution she has taken

( Prom Ike Liberal.) ft will bo seen by an advertisement in this impression that Captain llaasloff, in compliance with the recommendation of the meeting of Merchants and others at the Commercial Hall on Monday, proposes to hold a General Public Meeting of the Inhabitants on Friday next, at the Court House, for the purpose of laying before them the project of establishing a line ol Submarine Telegraph between the V est Indies and the Continent of America, to connect with the Transatlantic line. ( Prom the same.) A Public Meeting of Merchants and other leading Citizens was held on Monday forenoon at the Commercial Hall, P. Kilkelly, Esq., in the Chair, to hear from Captain Raasloff an exposition of the project of laying down a lino of Submarine Telegraph between the \\ est Indies and the American continent, to connect with the Transatlantic line. The meeting listened with a good deal of interest to Captain RaaslofFs plain statement of the object and aim of the projectors in seeking onr support, and the advantages to result to these Colonies, and especially to this Island, from the success ful carrying out of the project. One or two questions were interpellated at the close of Captain Raasloffs address by gentlemen pro sent for further explanation, which was satis factorily afforded, on points ol' interest. M r. Rennie made a few very terse and appropriate remarks in support of the project, on moving the first of the following Resolutions, which were all agreed to unanimously. Moved by Mr. Rennie, seconded by Mr. F A. Clairmonte. Resolved 1st þÿ That this meeting views with pleasure the plan of Telegraphic commit nication submitted by Captain Raasloff to his this Excellency which Island, the Governor, and Legislature ot in their opinion promises to be of immense benefit to the West Indies generally and to Barbados particularly, that they respectfully and urgently request and his Excellency the Governor and Legislature will give to it their immediate and earnest eon sideration and support.

Moved by Mr. W. 15. Griffith, seconded by Mr. John Heyes. Resolved 2nd þÿ That the Agricultural Interest of the Island be invited to co-operate with the Commercial in bringing about the objects of the meeting. Moved by Mr. G. Winter, seconded by Mr

The Deputation waited to-day, by appointment, upon the Governor, at the Court House, and placed the Resolutions and the views of the Meeting before him, when his Excellency made the following reply : þÿ þÿ Gentlemen, þÿ It has afforded me much gratification to witness the energy with which the Inhabitants of Bridgetown have taken up the groat project of uniting the West India Colonies with the Continents of North and South America, and through the former with Europe, by a submarine telegraph line. þÿ You may rely on my cordial support to a measure which 1 am persuaded will be most beneficial to the inhabitants of this Island of all classes ; but I must earnestly recommend you not to relax your exertions, but to endea- I vour to unite public opinion in favor of the project. Ultimate success will depend much on the co-operation of the most important West Indian Colonies, and should harmonious action take place on this occasion, I am not without hope, that it may be beneficially extended to other objects of common þÿinterest.

( From the I Vest Indian , Feb. 27.) Public attention has been occupied during the last fortnight with Captain llaaslofTs scheme of a West India Electric Telegraph and Mr. Sackersþÿdorf Submarine of the Careenage ; both of which have excited s blasting, for the improvement J much interest, the former from its prospective advantages, the latter from its immediate effects. Captain ltaasloff has achieved a great success, lie arrived hero by the last steamer from St. I Thomas and immediately laid his plan before the Governor and Legislature ; he then explained it at a meeting of the Merchants, held a few days after at the Commercial Hall, and again on Friday last at a general meeting of the inhabitants at the Town Gall. With the aid of the Press placed at his disposal, and cheerfully enlisted in the promotion of bis views, he was thus enabled to lay before the public of Barbados the principal features of the plan, the objects it contemplated, I and the advantages to be derived from it. By j this means he has obtained the unanimous support of the people of Barbados towards the accomplishment of the great object in view þÿ the union of j the two continents of North and South America, j by means of a Telegraph Line through the British and Danish West India Islands, the ceutre of which to be the island of St. Thomas, and the extremities two points not yet fixed on, one on the eastern or Atlantic coast of the United States, and the other on the Spanish Main. For the details of this grand scheme, which is

only a matter talked of and contemplated at present, wo refer to the reports of the proceedings at these Meetings, especially of the last, where will be found not only an interesting account of the Telegraph by Captain Kaasloff, but also an expression of tile opinion of Mr. Sealy, Mr. Taylor, and other gentlemen filling a prominent station here in favor of it. It is quite unnecessary for us to say anything on the subject ; the opinion of the public has been formed and expressed by what was said at these Meetings, and j we have been content to act merely as Reporters, seeing that this way was the most useful in promoting the success of the end in view. On Tuesday last, the House of Assembly unanimously concurred in a vote of ,£2, 500 a ! year towards the support of the Telegraph, that being considered a fair contribution for Barbados, to make up £7,000, which is proposed to be contributed by the British West India colonies, þÿthro which the line will pass. The Resolutions agreed to by the House are as follow, and the Message of the Governor recommending the project for their adoption : þÿ His Excellency the Governor, to His Honor the Speaker and House of Assembly. The Governor has the honor to inform the Honorable House of Assembly, with reference to his message of the 10th instant, that he has been requested by a Public Meeting held in the city of Bridgetown, on Friday the 20th instant, to

s t - c R 0 II X A\ V I S , bring the subject of the Submarine Telegraph specially before the Legislature at its next meeting. The Governor being deeply sensible of the vast importance of the contemplated project, trusts that the House of Assembly will guarantee the annual appropriation of a sum of money for the purpose of securing to Barbados the advantage of being one of the þÿCompany stations s as well as the transmission of messages containing commercial and general information to the extent of the appropriation. F. HINCKS- Government House, Barbados, Feb. 24, 1857. Resolved 1st þÿ That this House has learned with much satisfaction, that a project has been formed of uniting North and South America, and the principal West India Islands, by a Submarine Telegraph Line. 2nd þÿ That in the event of a Company being formed within a reasonable time with the capital necessary to carry out this project, this House will be ready to co-operate with the other branches of the Legislature in affording it the necessary protection, and such privileges within this colony as are usually given to Incorporated Companies. 3rd þÿ That if the British Government should enter into an agreement for a term of years with the proposed West India, North and South American Company, Under which, after the completion of the lino, and during its maintenance in working order, the Government should undertake to pay to the Company an annual sum of £7,000, being a moiety of the sum of £14,000, (the interest at 4 per cent, on the assumed

capital of £350,000), this House will be prepared to guarantee, on behalf of the colony of Barbados, if made one of the þÿCompany S s tations, such annual sum, not exceeding £2.500, as may be finally determined on, ns its proper share of the general contribution ot £7,000 per annum Jrotn the British West India colonies, being the other moiety of the proposed sum of £14, i 00, þÿ such sum of £14,000 being a fixed remuneration to the Company for the work done on behalf of the Government and the colonies in the c inveyance, outward and homeward, of Government messages, including Commercial and general information for the use of the Public. It being understood that this colony shall have the benefit in proportion to its contribution of the proposal, that the annual sum of £7,000 contributed by the colonies shall be reduced to £4,000 as soon as the net profits of the Company are equal to a Dividend ot 6 per cent. And also, that if the number of Stations in the W, st Indies be increased, the sum contributed by the colony or colonies, in which they may be established, ge in diminution of the sura .contributed by the others. We shall only further remark, that we hopo the example of Barbados in s > readily giving I r countenance and support to the scheme, may weigh with the Legislatures of the other C denies to take part in it likewise The advantages to be derived from its accomplishment are as great to them as to us, especially in the case of Trinidad, which is regarded as the outlet for a large

portion of the trade and commerce of the neighbouring State of Venezuela. If it is a necessity for Barbados, to enable her to keep her position in the Islands, it is no less necessary for Trinidad to give her a hold upon the trade of the immense district of the Orinoque. Otherwise, supposing the Telegraph to pass direct from St. Thomas to La Guayra, and not through the Antilles, Trinidad would be deprived of most of the advantages of her position at the mouth of that great river. It is the intention of Captain Kaasloff to leave for Trinidad in a day or two, we understand, and afterwards to visit the other Islands, which he proposes to make stations of and to obtain contributions from, for the support of the line. lie has left at the Commercial Hall specimens of the submarine cable, and of that used in the Land Telegraph, for the inspection of the curious. The foi tner has the appearance of a rope plaited ot iron threads ; which are wrapped round a body of gutta pereha ; and in the gutta percha are one : or more small copper wires. The land cable consists only of the gutta percha rope enclosing the wires. It is the wire which transmits the electrio current ; for which purpose one is sufficient, but more wires are used in case of injury j10 one. In the submarine cable the outer coverlnR of iron wires is required to protect the gutta Pcrcha rope and the copper wires from injury.

Literature in China. þÿ The Chinese booksellers have an odd way of selling their volumes þÿ according to weight. THE EFFECTS OF DRAINING. Professor Norton says : When the drain is þÿ made and covered, the water which falls upon the ground does not remain to stagnate, and does not run away over the surface, washing off the best of the soil, but sinks gradually down, yielding to 'be roots of plants any fertilizing matter which it may contain, and often washing out some hurtful substances. As it descends, air and warmth follow it. Under these n w influences, the proper decompositions and preparation of compounds fit for the sustenau e of plants go on, the soil is warm j by washing hurtful substances out of and sufficiently dry, and plants flourish which formerly never would grow on it in if at all. It is a curious fact, too, that such soils assist drouth better than ever before.

The reason is, that the plants are able to send their roots much farther down in search of food, without finding any thing hurtful. Every part being penetrated witli air, and consequent- in ly drier and lighter, these soils do not bake summer, but remain mellow and porous. Such effects can not, in their full extent, be looked for in a stiff clay, during the first season j the change must be gradual, but it is þÿsure. The effects of draining are thus enumerated by Professor Johnson. þÿ 1 It Causes the Air to be Renewed. þÿ It is believed that the admission of frequently renewed supplies of air into the soil is favorable to its fertility. This the descent of the rain promotes. When it falls upon the soil it makes its way into the pores and fissures, expelling of course the air which previously filled them. When the rain ceases, the water runs off by the drains ; and ns it leaves the pores of the soil empty above it, the air follows, and fills with a renewed supply the numerous cavities fr.im which the descent of the rain had driven it. Where land remains full of water, no such renewal of air can take place. þÿ 2. It Warms the Under Soil þÿ As the rain falls through the nir, it acquires the temperature of the atmosphere. If this be highe than that of the surface soil, the latter is wanned by it ; if the rains be copious, and sink easily into the subsoil, they will carry this warmth with them to the depth of the drains. 'I bus the under soil in well-drained land is not only

warmer because the evaporation is less, out because the rains in the summer season actually bring down warmth from the heavens to their natural heat. þÿ 3. It Equalizes a the Temperature of the Soil iil the fceason of þÿGrowth. T he sun upou surface of the soil, and gradually warms it. Yet, even a few rect heat descends only in summer, this di- inches beneath the surface. But when the rain falls upon the warm surface, and finds an easy descent, as it does in open soils, it becomes itself warmer and carries its heat down to the under soil. The former, in particular, has, 1 understand, been charged by his Government to urge on the Shah the necessity of ratifying the treaty which has been negotiated in Paris, and the draught of which has been submitted to the English Government, and otherwise to co-operate to the utmost of his power towards the satisfactory solution of the question. If Russian influence be not uppermost when the treaty is received at Teheran it will be ratified; if otherwise, the chances are, as I have already mentioned, agninst us. ASTRONOMY. With much pleasure we give insertion in our columns to the subjoined communication of Major Andrew Lang, accompanying two highly interesting Lectures on Astronomy, delivered in Scotland by one of the most eminent Astronomers of the age. We regret, however, that the length of the Lectures and the limits of our sheet prevent our publishing them both at once ; we, therefore, make room for the first Lecture to-day, and in our next we will produce the second. In recommending them for perusal, we endorse the sentiments put forth by our scientific correspondent, except in so far as their being the greatest ornament that we have ever made public. As the astronomer loves the science of Astronomy, and deems everything connected with it the most interesting, so does the agriculturist consider matters relating to agriculture the most worthy of attention ; and every one else, in his turn, will view subjects of interest to himself as best adapted to all. To the Editor of the St. Croix þÿ þÿAvis. Slit, By the last Mail, a Lady in Scotland sent me the Kilmarnock þÿ Weekly þÿPost of the j 31st January last, in which is contained the I substance of two Lectures on Astronomy, delivered there by Mr. Lee, F. R. S. and F. R. A S., and not only a Fellow of the Royal As- j tronomical Society of London, but lately, anil may be still, as Vice President, þÿ a situation to which none but the most eminent men could aspire. With unmixed pleasure and satisfaction I have read these two lectures, as containing a

complete Epitome of Astronomy, delivered in the best language, and in a manner to be perfectly comprehended by every sensible person, and I have no hesitation in recommending their insertion into the St. Croix Avis, as the greatest ornament it has ever made public. My opinion is that your paper containing these two lectures should be obtained by every well-informed individual in the community, and I request that for myself you will furnish me with ten copies to be used at my discretion. I am, Sir, Your obedient servant, ANDW. LANG, F. It A. S. þÿEliza Retreat, s 12th March, 1857.

A Race Across the Atlantic. þÿ Tlie United States mail steamship Atlantic left New York for Liverpool on the 1st, inst. Among the passengers was a man named Winter (with his wile), a clerk of a mercantile firm in that city, having in tiis possession 2,000 dollars belonging to his employers, and which lie had obtained by breaking open the safe. < hi his absence being ascertained together with the amount of money with which lie had absconded, the principal of the firm obtained a warrant for bis apprehension, and tuok a passage by the British and North American mail steamship Persia, three days afterwards The chance were in favour of the criminal clerk; for though the Persia is the fastest steamer afloat, it could scarcely be expected that she would overtake a full-powered steamer, which sailed three days betorc her. No sign of the pursued steamer was seen until off the port, when the Persia came up with and passed her, arriving in the river two hours before her. On Mr. Hood, the gi utlemen who hoards the Ounard steamers to take charge of the mails, going aboard, he was introduced to the pursuing merchant, who asked, with some anxiety, if any one had landed from tlie Atlantic. On tiring answered in the negative, he stated the case, and asked for u detective. Subsequently, aecom anted by a police-officer, he boarded tbe Atlantic, and confronted the astounded Winter, whose dreams of security were tints rudely dissipated. The steamer Ca'eufta arrived at Trieste on Wednesday, having started from Alex- | andria at three p. in. on the Gth of Alurch. At Hong-Kong 1111' attempt made to poison the European community had caused great consternation ; one of the partners in u Chinese bakery had been arrested and committed for trial, with nine other Chinese. Admiral Seymour, tit Canton, had withdrawn form the Factory gardens and the Dutch Folly. In reply to the treacherous attempts made by the Chinese against British life and property, the western suburbs of Canton had been burnt down. Intelligence from Bushire had been received to the 23rd of January. The general health of the army was good, and the supplies were plentiful. No military operation had been undertaken. General : Outratn had not yet arrived. The conferences between Sir John Lawrence and Dost Mohammed broke up on the 28th January, when the Ameer departed for Cabul. Ii was asserted that a British Residency was about to be established at Candahar. The Paris correspondent of the Morning Post says : þÿ There is every reason to believe, from the character of the despatches and private letters coming from China, that the war is not likely to terminate so soon as might be hoped. It is evident, also, that a consider-

able naval and military force must be on the watch for some time to come to protect the lives of Europeans, even when hostilities have ceased. The authorities of Pekin have both publicly and privately instructed the Celestials to stab and poison þÿ in fact, possess themselves of the persons of the Barbarians by any means which their ingenious minds can suggest. It results, therefore, that at all the ports where Europeans reside by virtue of the Treatv

of 1842, foreigners have either taken refuge on board ship, or forces have been landed tor their protection. Ere long augmented naval and military resources will reach the Chinese waters ; and it is proposed to occupy Chinese territory, which will afford a material guarantee in hand to treat with "the Son of Heaven," as we ought to call the Emperor of China. Meanwhile it is reported at Canton that Tartar troops and an extensive navy of junks are to attack and drive away the invaders of the Celestial Empire. It was also said that Russia had offered assistance to the Emperor. At all events it is pretty evident that we are again in for a Chinese war, and, if properly carried out, it is perhaps a fortunate event. Sooner or later it must have taken place. Hitherto we have never succeeded in making the Chinese authorities observe treaties. Ic has been proved that the Celestial Government has little control over its distant and inferior agents ; hence the origin of continual grievances wirh foreigners, and hence the cause, it is asserted, of the widespread rebellion winch has been smouldering since 1852. I'he " Triad," or secret societies, exist throughout the empire, and their aim is to overthrow lie present Tartar dynasty, and reform the existing oppressive and corrupt system of government. Under such circumstances the present European demonstration may be fraught with great events, although we hear the Imperialists and rebels have joined to oppose the English ex-

pedition. It is, however, exceedingly difticult to form a correct idea of Chinese politics, or know what is passing in the heart of the empire. The Jesuits know more about ( 'liina than any one else. They and Russia (which Power contrived some time since to form anomalous relations with I'ckiii) are the only sources for internal information. The Jesuits have been long since admitted to 1'ekin tor scientific reasons þÿ in fact, they make the astronomical calculations tor the Chinese Government, daily have been murdered ; but some have r 'turned to Europe, and bring with them, it is reported, most valuable information. 1 bit as the publicity of this information might prevent future intercourse it is not likely to be given to the world. Nevertheless 1 am told the Jesuits declare a complete convulsion is inevitable. The Chinese arc said to be essentially unbelievers in any firm of religion whatever, and society is in the most, demoralised condition. Many of the Jesuits are declared to have fallen victims to Chinese cruelty and bad faith.

We some time ago announced the appointment of a commission to proceed from Martinique to Cuba, for the purpose of investigating Dr. Humboldt's alleged discovery of a means of preventing yellow fever by inoculation. The report made by that commission has never fallen under our observation, but we find in the official columns of the Moniteur of Martinique what appears to be a pretty conclusive expose by M. Berg, surgeon of the French brig of war Meleagre. The European journals per last packet make mention also of the discovery. We proceed to lay before our readers all that has reached us on the subject, beginning with the European account : þÿ " the the Gazette Medicate " According to a statement recently made in yellow fever may be prevented in the ma- ," says a London paper, jority of instances by previous inoculation with the diluted virus of a reptile. The statement is made by Dr. Lucien Papilland, who, at die period of announcement, had performed no less than 2477 inoculations on persons living in districts ravaged by yellow fever, and with the most satisfactory results. Only 288 or 10 per cent, of the number inoculated were subsequently attacked by yellow fever, though exposed to its influence ; 68 per cent, of the total number, or per cent., died ; 2247, or 90 per cent , were altogether projected. Dr. Papilland calculates that no less than 16 per cent, of the total population of a region infested by yellow fever may

be preserved by his mode of preventive treatment. The history of the discovery is not a little singular. .Some time since Dr. (J. Humboldt announced the fact that the inhabitants of Central America were liable to be bitten in the feet and legs by a reptile of undetermined species. Many died in consequence, but those who survived remained singularly free from the ravages of yellow fever. M. Papillaud inoculates with the diluted poison of the reptile, which he irritates until it biles a piece of sheep's liver ; and the juice of the latter thus impregnated is the material employed for inoculation." In La France d' Ovtre-Mer, (Martinique paper) of the 3rd instant, the whole affair is brought into disparagement, as shewn below : þÿ 11 Our readers will doubtless remember the preservative inoculation invented by a medical practitioner of Havana, of the celebrated name of Humboldt, by which it was promised that humanity should be relieved for ever of one of its most dreadful scourges, the yellow fever. We have from time to time published several articles upon this subject, which so vitally interests all the West India Colonies, including a remarkable letter which was addressed to us by a friend at Havana, Dr. Gaudon Ilulain. Some time after, the Government of our Colony, with the laudable object of possessing itself of a process which promised such happy results, sent a medical commission to study on the spot the practice of Dr. Humboldt, and this commission has made known

the result of its observations through the local Moniteur. Although all those documents do not conclude in favour of the Havaua Doctor's process, much of anxiety has hitherto prevailed, in this igland at least, as to the real value of the antidotal inoculation. But now, thanks to the equally clear and positive report of M. Berg, late surgeon-major of the brig Meleagre, who last year sojourned at Havana, we are enabled to remove all hesitation from the minds of our readers. Unfortunately, we are also under the necessity of declaring that no serious thought needs henceforth bo given to the process, it having in nowise realised the expectations of its author. Thus, at least, is it judged by Dr. Berg of the navy, who states þÿ " ' At Havana, I in the first place hastened to see M. de Humboldt. That, practitioner offered to furnish every information I should desire, atd authorised one to visit frequently his sick house at Garini. (Casa de salud por la. inoculation preservation de In fiebre amarilla.) The inoculations had been recently suspended on account of the cholera uniting its ravages to those of the yellow fever. M de Humboldt was then awaiting the termination of the epidemio in Novem-

s em i & v ii s ber 1855 to resume bis experiments, although his process, he told me, was a sure preservative against all miasmatic affections, such as the cholera, which he considered as identical, from its nature and origin, with the American typhus. " ' I will not discuss M de Humboldt's ideas on the uature of yellow fever, which, according to him, is characterised only by the black or hemorrhagic vomit ; nor on the non-reproduction of the malady in a person who has previously suffered from it. Clinical observations are opposed to the former opinion ; and the latter cannot be sustained in presence of the numerous facts which all of us witness daily. At iny request, M. de Humboldt, placed me in possession of the figures showing the results of his trials: þÿ Fiom 18th Dec. 1854, to 1st Nov. 1855. Entered for Deaths Deaths febrile af- from yel- from tyfections. low fever, phoid fever. Inoculated . 3.000. ..575 19 3 Non-inoculated. 461 ...323 167 19 It was interesting to learn exactly the nature of the 676 febril affections which claimed anew the care of M. de Ilumboldt. According to him, they were remittent or intermittent; but 1 must remark, that in the theory of that practitioner, intermittent fever is but the first stage of the yellow fever, " This favourable statistic relates, however, 4 only to the sailors and soldiers attended in the military hospital of Havana, a large establishment previously given up to M. de Humboldt as a theatre for his official experiments. In town, a crowd of newly arrived Europeans were attracted

to the sick-house at Garcini, to get themselves inoculated, at the rate of a doubloon each. "'The matter of the inoculation, which was shewn me, has been correctly described by the Commission from Martinique; but all my efforts to obtain a view of one of the reptiles said to be so common, proved useless. M. de Humboldt told me that he had just shipped his last reptile to the Medical Society of Bordeaux, and that he expected others from Mexico. I applied to a number of apothecaries of the town, all of whom were astonished at my request, stating that the joke had been long ago exploded. " ' It became necessary that I should thenceforth pursue my inquiries amongst the other Doctors oi Havaua, and I accordingly applied to several recommendable ones. I received the best possible welcome from the Dean of the Faculty of Medical Sciences, Dr. Gastrovcrdo, who authorised me to use his name ; from the Doctors of the Spanish Army and Navy ; and from two French Doctors, Belot brothers, who enjoyed a merited reputation at Havana From them 1 learnt how little foundation there was for the first announcement of the benefits of the inoculation ; the regiment of Zaratoga continued to lose the gre iter part of its people by yellow fever, which the inoculation could not put a stop to. The small four-limbed serpent ( le petit serpent a. quart re mcmhres rudimentairrs) could neither be procured nor seen at Havana, and the New Orleans journals recorded the fruitless researches of the medical men of Vera Cruz, who could never

set hands upon this miraculous animal. " The body of practitioners of Cuba, it must be confessed, shewed the most violent opposition " to M. de Ilumboldt. I resolved upon visiting the hospitals, to endeavour to obtain explicit information upon the subject. At the younger Dr. Belot's, 1 saw, in 74 cases of yellow fever, 15 men inoculated ; on board the frigate Cortez, 220 had been inoculated, 90 died of the yellow fever. At the San-Francisco hospital, from 9th July to 31st December 1855, there had been admitted 389 sick, exclusively from French merchant-ships; out of that number, 190 wero attacked by yellow fever, and all of these had undergone inoculation. In the same hospital, there were 16 previously inoculated persons attacked by the cholera, against which they should have been preserved according to the pretensions of M. de Humboldt, yet of that number 7 deaths were recorded. " ' Those facts could not reach the knowledge of the public, as the authorities of Cuba, who patronized M de Humboldt's essays, had forbidden the publication of all information upon unfavourable results. Nevertheless, the truth did come to light, and towards the close of my residence at Havana (February 1756), M. de Humboldt had ceased to practise the inoculation; the yellow fever raged everywhere, in town,

amongst the shipping, and in the hospitals. The old methods of treatment, had had to be resumed, and the most sanguine partisans of inoculation no longer hesitated to acknowledge the disappointment of their hopes.'"

Bahama. þÿ Treasury Frauds. þÿ The Bahama Royal Gazette of the 24th of January, lent us by a respected subscriber, gives the following account of criminal proceedings against the Receiver General and Treasurer of Bahama, on three distinct charges of embezzlement of the public money. General Court þÿ Yesterday being the day fixed for the trial of G. O. Smith, lately Receiver General and Treasurer, against whom several informations had been filed during the present term, the Court was crowded with spectators. The former respectability of the prisoner, and the fact of his having for so many years held such responsible situations, in which he appeared to have possessed the entire confidence of the government and the public, were the cause <>f much anxiety to know the particulars of the charges against him, and the proofs by which they were likely to be supported. At 10 o'clock the prisoner was place 1 at the bar, and having pleaded not guilty to the information read, proceed d, unassisted by Counsel, to conduct hiown case. He commenced by challenging a great number of jurors, but twelve wero at last impanelled. The Attorney General then addressed the Court and Jurv on the information which charged the prisoner with three, distinct acts of embezzlement of the public money, to the amount altogether of £522 18s. lid, committed by him while R eeiver General and Treasurer. The respective sums were alleged to have been paid to the prisoner by merchants in liquidation of their bonds due to the Treasury for import du-

ties, but were not credited to the Colony. The substance of the Prisoner' defence was, that between the years 1842 and 1S46, losses had been sustained in the Treasury Department through notes in circulation, but that such losses really occurred, or how they occurred, he offered no proof but a memorandum of his own handwriting, He also stated that some years ago he lost a number of cheques on the Bank, amounting to <£U 00, the drawers of which with one exception, he did not remember, in support of which assertion, he called \V. J. Weech, Esquire, merchant, and \V. II. Hall, Esquire, cashier of the Bank, hut these gentlemen proved only that the former gave and the latter paid on oar occasion a duplicate cheque, for one which the prisoner said he had lost. II cnnelud. d with an impassioned appeal to the feelings of the jury, urging his great dipt re.-.- of mind and the misery which would be caused to his family We re gretted to hear him do this, as in our opinion, such appeals ought not to be made to or regarded by a jury, whose sworn duty it is, to pronounce their verdict strictly in accordance with the evidence, without allowing cither indignation on the one hand, or compassion on the other, to influence them. After a brief reply from the Attorney-General, in the sumo tone and spirit as his opening speech, and an impartial summing up by t-lio Court, the jury retired for about a quarter of an hour, and returned with a verdict of guilty. The Court then adjourned until this morning,

when it was expected that one or more of the remaining informations would be proceeded with; but after the prisoner had been placed at the bar, the Attorney-General announced that it was not his intention to prosecute on the other informations, and that he thought the ends of justice would be attained by asking the Court tor judgment on the verdict returned yesterday. The Chief Justice then sentenced the prisoner to be imprisoned for two years with hard labour. Thus terminated these important proceedings, which have excited such a painful interest in the community. On the unhappy delinquent himself, it is unnecessary to make any lengthened remarks. His misdeeds have been the cause of much misery to himself and others, and many years will elapse before their effects will cease to be felt. We hope that his fate will be a warning to any who are disposed to deviate from the path of rectitude, that justice, though sometimes slow, is ever sure to overtake offenders. As a learned Judge in England remarked a short time ago, when sentencing the London Bankers, Paul Sf Co., "such cases should convince all men of the necessity of praying that they may not be led into temptation."

We have transferred to the columns of our present issue such extracts of European and other politics as we could not make room for in our last publication. The China War appears to be the chief subject engaging the attention of the British Government and People at the present time. The attempts made by the inhabitants of Hong Kong to poison the British community had not resulted in such fatal consequences as was intended, owing to the large quantities of arsenic used, which acted generally as a violent emetic. The head man of a bakery, after disposing of his poisoned bread, had made his escape for Macao, There was some delay on the part of the Government in sending after him, but a private gentleman, a sufferer from the atrocious attempt, chartered a steamer, and succeeded in capturing the baker before he landed at Macao. He was taken back to Hong Kong to stand his trial, together with several other men who had been employed on the premises. These and other atrocities are evidence of the Chinese having no claim to be considered civilized people. Shot and shell, and men to use them, had been sent from England to Admiral Seymour, who was strengthening his position for some decisive steps. Commissioner Yeh had addressed a letter to the United States Minister, asking him why he had not ordered all American subjects and American ships of war away from Hong Kong, to be clear of the present troubles. It was believed that the British Admiral would no longer show any forbearance to the
Chinese, but would without delay bring them to a proper sense of their atrocious proceedings.

THE WAR IN CHINA. The official despatches received by the last Overland Mail from Sir John Bowring and Sir Michael Seymour give accounts of the attack made upon the British shipping by a vast number of Chinese junks. The attack, which was well concerted, being made at low water, when the larger men-of-war could not safely manoeuvre, was brilliantly repelled. Sir Michael Seymour had thought it wise to abandon his posts at the Dutch Folly and the Factory Gardens, and had strengthened his positions at forts lower down ihe river. Five hundred men were expected from Singapore.

RUSSIA AND PERSIA. Constantinople, March 2. A Russian corps of 3,000 men had been received with enthusiasm at Tabriz. The Persian army destined to act against the Affghans had been reinforced ; and Russia was seeking to occupy the Khanate ofKhoukhand, with a view to the extension of its frontier to the English possessions. The Sovereign of Bokhara, alarmed at these projects of invasion on the part of Russia, had solicited tlie mediation of the Sultan to secure the independence of Khoukhand.

A Ministerial journal, in announcing that the Spanish Minister at Mexico had not been able to obtain the satisfaction which he demanded, and had left for Cuba, says: þÿ þÿ Vera Cruz and all the coast are already blockaded by our forces, and soon the Mexicans will learn to their expense that the honour and interests of Spain are not to he trifled with. Diplomatic arrangements, it is true, are talked of, hut it is not to he supposed that the Spanish Government will now yield the smallest of its pretensions ; it calls for a just and complete schakoff reparation, and it must obtain it. The fleet to he sent from Spain to act against
Isabel II., line-of-hattle-ship, the Bailen frigate, the Pelago brig, and the Colon Moldavian frontier, so as to create a steamer, have arrived at Cadiz, which

Several French officers have demanded permission from the Emperor to join þÿsure. the expedition, and in some few cases this permission has been granted. The Government learns that the American Government looks with extreme disfavour on this expedition. General de Laroche, the Governor of Girona, and General Garrido, who holds a high command in the province of Aragon, have volunteered to proceed to Cuba. All the troops that are as yet known to he under orders for Cuba are about 2,000 men, draughts from different regiments, and which in any case would he sent later in the year to fill up the vacancies caused by deaths and completion of service in the ranks of the army in the Spanish West Indies- It is asserted, however, that in addition to these, a sufficient body of troops could he spared from Cuba to form the expedition against Mexico. Lafragua, an agent of the Mexican Government, had arrived at Southampton on his way to Madrid, to give explanations in the name of that Government on the events that have recently taken place in Mexico, of which Spain complains.

The appointment of the blustrous old enemy of England, General Cass, to the Secretaryship for Foreign Affairs in President þÿBuchanan s forthcoming Administration is regarded with interest, we will not say with anxiety, on both shies of the water. Our late disputes with the United States have taught us more of that community, as it lias become under recent changes, than we could else have been expected to know. We can estimate at its true value the entire amount of bluster and pretence. We know that Jonathan not only enjoys his own loud talk, hut moreover expects to get something by it in imposing upon others. The Union , a Washington Democrat paper supposed to be connected with the new Government, atfects to resent our very presence in Central America altogether, blames those of its countrymen who joined with our Ministry in the treaty that was to have secured the neutrality of the great projected ship canal, and claims the transit between the oceans as the peculiar and individual concern of the Republic. The writer is well answered by the New York journalists, that we happened to have rights in Central America before the treaty, while the United States had none ; that we h ive very graciously conceded all the points of them that might give us powers of aggression ; and that, in fact, it was we who accepted the States as sharers in our own more immediate concerns. Be all this as it may, while Canada belongs to Great Britain, this empire is as much an American power as the
Great Republic itself. It is not at this moment that any considerable traffic is carried on between our continental ports

on the Atlantic and þÿVancouver Island, s and our other Pacific seahord ; hut who dreamed, a dozen years ago, of the intercourse which the New Yorkers now hold with San Francisco? What Englishman is ready to give up now the very probable advantage of a continental Pacific route between this country and Australasia? The lately negotiated treaty between the two countries is held in suspense for ratification, modification, or rejection by the Senate, to he decided under the Buchanan administration. It is not very likely t hat, after having given up Ruatan to Honduras, (lie matter of most consequence in dispute, we shall leave the Americans any cause for serious, candid discontent in any renewal of negotiations. Moreover, it may be, as alleged, that General (hiss only joins Mr. þÿBuchanan Ministry s to inaugurate it with the benefit of his reputation, being of years to make retirement more desirable to him than office. Mr. Gold), who is already pointed out as likely to succeed him, and who begins as Secretary to the 'Treasury, is known as a man of moderate views. Against all this we have to set Mr. þÿBuchanan Ostend s manifesto, and that farewell speech at the Lord þÿMayor dinner s which some of our cotemporaries greeted as so very amicable, hut which they soon saw, with ourselves, was only a warning to England, that it would he wise in her to keep quiet. And, as an element among the chances, we must not absolutely forget John þÿBull s present very pugnacious disposition. He is angry with

himself, as well as with all about him; and if any real injury should arise ta give him a subject on which he can wreak his wrath, with the unanimous approbation of his family, it is not impossible that he may even think the provocation a piece of good fortune. We hope for a quieter disposition on all sides before the treaty is again discussed in London, and, above all, we trust to that great community of interest and feeling which hinds the two Anglo-Saxon nations, and which would make any contest between them appear as unnatural as a war between the Southern and the Northern States of the Republic.

An Accident which, though comic enough, might easily have had a tragical ending, occurred the other day at Ma- Tussaud's Exhibition. A medical student, examining the guillotine in the Chamber of Horrors, took it into his head that the sort of yoke which fits down on the shoulders of the criminal to hold him in his place would not he sufficient to confine a person who strug gled. His curiosity on this point led liiui to watch till the place was empty, when lie actually put himself in, letting down the yoke. He soon tound that he was quite unable to lift it, and it at once flashed into his mind that the sharp axe which was suspended over his neck could not he very firmly fixed, or it would not fall (as it does) with a touch, lie was afraid to struggle, lest the shaking should bring it down and at once deposit his head in the basket of sawdust below him, into which his eyes were of necessity steadily looking. Having stayed some time in this plight, lie was overjoyed to hear t lie approach of a visitor whom he suppliantly implored to release him "I'm thinking," said the gentleman (a Scotch visitor of the metropolis) to his wife ; " I'm thinking he must be hired to show how the thing acts, and I think we'd better not interfere." So the luckless student was left till M Tussaud came in, and made fast the axe before releasing him. The axe has been removed and laid by the side to prevent future accidents.

The Present Parliament. þÿ The present Parliament, which is Ihe fourth Parliament of Queen Victoria, and the sixth of the " Reformed" Parliaments, was elected in July 152, under the auspices of the Earl of Derby, then at the head of the Conservative Administration. It would not, according to the Septennial Act, die a natural death till the 25th of August, 1859 (the day at which the writs of the new Parliament were made returnable), but since the year 1828 no Parliament, according to Mr. Dotl, lias appro iclied its extreme limit. The present Parliament, if dissolved without any material delay, will have failed to attain the age of live years liy some four or five mm llis. The Russell Parliament, elected in July and August, 1847, lasted four years seven months and 12 d ivs, and the Parliament which placed the late Sir Robert Peel in office in the year 1841, lasted as long as five years and 1 1 months, or very nearly six years. This was the longest of the Reformed Parliaments, the shortest having been the first, elected at the end of the year 1832, the age of which was one year and II months only. It will he found that the average duration of the six Reformed Parliaments elected from 1832 to 1852 lias been, as nearly as possible, four years supposing the present Parliament to be dissolved this spring.

The .Ten British Minister. his interview with the deputation of the chamber of commerce þÿ his democratic personal appearance and manner þÿ lady napier, etc., etc. Lord Napier, the new British Minister to Washington, is still stopping at the Clarendon, where he intends to remain until his departure for Washington on Tuesday morning. Owing occur that his departure would to a supposition sooner, he has been left in comparative quiet, very much to his satisfaction. On Saturday afternoon he was waited upon by a deputation, provided for at the last meeting of the Chamber of Commerce, to tender to his lordship on his arrival the cordial congratulations of that body. The deputation consisted of Peletiah Perit, Esq., President of the Chamber ; Moses H. Cfrinnell, J. T. King, Alexander Duncan, Thomas Tileston, A. Norrie, II. A. Coit, J. De Peyster Ogden, John A Stephens, and a number of influential merchants invited by the committee. Upon entering the room the chairman was introduced to his lordship, who was also made acquainted with the other members of the deputation. Mr. Perit, the chairman, then addressed his lordship as follows: þÿ On behalf of the Chamber of Commerce of the city of New York, we have come to pay our respects to you, and to offer to you, your lady and family, a cordial welcome to the shores of America, and in doing which we would give utterance to the sentiments and feelings of the whole community. Your arrival in this country is more interesting, as it fully restores the diplomatic

relations between Great Britain and the United States, and will, we trust, be the means of adding strength to the ties of consanguinity, friendship and interest which now bind these nations together. On this continued harmony of feeling and action depend not only the prosperity ot two great and powerful nations, but the advancement of commerce, civilization and liberal institutions throughout the world. It will be the distinguished privilege of your mission, we trust, to contribute largely to these great objects. We regret that your early departure for Washington will prevent an opportunity of extending the attentions which we would have offered, together with our fellow citizens. We can only otfer you in this interview our hearty welcome. Lord Napier replied as follows ; þÿ Mr. Perit and Gentlemen þÿ I beg that you will convey to the New York Chamber of Commerce my high sense of the honor they have done me in offering me of their congratulations on the occasion my arrival in America. I can assure you that no efforts of mine shall be wanting to realize the happy anticipations you have had the goodness to express, and to deserve the favorable opinion which you have gratuitously formed of my ability to promote the true interests of our respective countries. I come with every desire to be useful. Although I have never visited America before, I have enjoyed the intimacy and friendship of many of your countrymen abroad, and I would gladly merit that regard on the part of the nation which has
been extended to me by its individual members. The sentiments of cordiality and good feeling which you have been pleased to convey to me, are those which animate

$ ? P 1 o |j & A) V D $« the government and people of Great Britain. I do not believe that during the temporary suspension and interruption of diplomatic intercourse those feelings ever ceased to exist. I am gratified to anticipate that nothing can more mar the harmony of our international relations or diminish those friendly sentiments in the hearts of our countrymen. I venture a hope that the period of my employment in the United States may be passed in that concord and co-operation which are so essential to the best interests of mankind. As each of the visitors was introduced his lordship shook him cordially by the hand, saying, " I am happy to see you, sir," and at the conclusion of the speeches he entered freely into conversation with those present. His personal appearance is in a " live lord." He is about five feet far different from what would be expected nine inches in height and dresses with democratic plainness. His hear is black, strongly intermixed with grey, though he does not appear to be over thirty-five years of age. II is large, searching dark eyes form a very conspicuous portion of his features. The expression of his face is somewhat that of a thorough businessman, and his manner, though slightly tinged with hauteur, is, ncverthelesss, quite cordial. He is, in fact, a very democratic lord. He dines at the table d'hote as a matter of preference, remarking that he wishes to become acquainted with the people of this country. In conversation he is peculiar. Like a good diplomatist, as he has the reputation

of being, he listens more than he speaks, and always has questions to ask. He has a sort of hesitancy in speech, seemingly caused by a desire to make a careful selection of language. His mind seems to have a practical turn, for he spoke of securing a house at Washington as soon as possible, and mentioned a desire to know the most pleasant residence in summer. He expressed his desire to present his credentials to the President as soon as possible. With an evident appreciation of the most difficult question likely to arise during his mission, Lord Napier was very inquisitive as to the position of General Walker in Central America, and as to the probable result of his operations He expressed his appreciation of the humanity of Morgan to Co. in refusing to carry more recruits & Walker and certain destruction. Lady Napier has already won the hearts of all who have hail the pleasure of her acquaintance. She is amiable and even affable in her manner, and exceedingly well fitted for an Ambassador's wife. She will remain with her children in Baltimore until suitable accommodations can be provided at Washington.

From a letter dated Canton, Jan. 15, in the Monitcur de la finite, we learn that the Chinese Government at Pekin has addressed the following instructions to the Governors of the five ports : þÿ 1. Until further orders, all the inhabitants of the Celestial Empire are prohibited from trading with the subjects of her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain. 2. The opium markets, which have been open for the trade of the two nations, are I provisionally subjected to some very severe regulations, closed. Allfgid Poisoning of British Subjects in China. þÿ The following communications were posted in the underwriters' room, Liverpool, on Monday last: þÿ Extract from a letter dated Hong-Kong, 15th Jan.: þÿ " I am hardly able to hold my pen to write you a few lines, being under the influence of a strong emetic taken to destroy the effects of poisoned bread at this morning's breakfast. Mr. , Mr. . and myself were seized with violent fits of vomiting immediately after leaving the table, and I have just been informed that the whole town is more or less affected in the same way, by bread which has been baked by a Chinese shopman. We are so surrounded by the scoundrels that it is hardly possible to guard against their designs, and the atrocious blood-money edicts issued by the Canton Government have ser on foot a system of assassination and kidnapping by no means pleasant. How this state of things will end it is impossible to say ; but, notwithstanding the injury to our interest, I cannot regret that the Canton people are at last about to meet their deserts. Trifling as was the original matter in dispute, the time must have come sooner or later when the humiliating position of foreigners could be no longer endured. At the other ports it is altogether different, and it will be a serious matter if they become closed against our trade, but I don't think they will. The exports of tea will be from 25,000.000 lb. to 30,000,- 000. deficient." Another letter savs : þÿ " The baker from whom the poisoned bread
was purchased is in custody, but it is feared legal difficulties will prevent a conviction. I mean to make my cook, a Chinaman, taste everything in mv presence before 1 partake of it."

The artesian well now being bored at Passy has already reached the depth of 510 metres, and in a few days, when the layer of stone that now lies between the diggers and the water is pierced, the work in this part will be accomplished. On the occasion of the bursting forth of the stream f rom the earth, the Emperor, with several other distinguished personages, proposes to be present to witness this really curious spectacle.
