BARBADOS. (From the West Indian, Feb. 24. ) Meeting on W. I Telegraph at Town Hall. The inhabitants of Barhodos were invited to attend at the town Hall on Friday last, to hear an explanation from Captain ltaasloff, of his project for laying Telegraph a Line through the West Indies. Only a few persons attended, amongst them however, were several gentlemen of station and influence, the, lion. G- þÿ E. Thomas, G. N. Taylor, Dr. Goding, of the Council ; Messrs. Lyall, Grant, Briggs and Simmons, of the Assembly ; Messrs. Kilkelly, Rennie, Atkins, Dr. Clarke, Stevens, Elder, Austin, G. Spencer, S. Taylor, and others. On the motion of Mr. Elder, seconded by Mr. Austin, the Hon. G. E. Thomas was called to the chair. Mr. Thomas said, that on this occasion he. was relieved of the usual duty of a Chairman, ; hardly to explain the objects of the Meeting, and to enlarge upon the topics connected with it,

S T , c R 0 | X A y c which would he done by Captain Raasloff a gentleman of considerable scientific attainments. The Electric Telegraph þÿ one of the most wonderful achievementsof inode i n science, than which there was none more wonderful in the history of the woild þÿ was the work of a subtle and mysterious agent, with the nature ami operations of which we were not yet fully acquainted. It was one of the hidden and marvellous instruments of Providence, with which we had only recently become acquainted, and the uses of which were still almost wholly concealed from us. It would be for Captain Raasloff, whom he begged to introduce to the Meeting to explain how ho proposed to accomplish his object, of uniting the the Continent of America, þÿ which if accomplished would form an epoch in the history of the West Indies ; what amount of money it was supposed to require, and how he proposed to raise the capital ; what advantages would follow from the establishment of the line. It was a subject of the highest importance, and he trusted that the meeting would give to it that attention which its importance demanded. Captain Raasloff said þÿ He had already addressed two Meetings in Bridgetown, and explained the principal features of i lie contemplated line. The Press of the Island had also assisted him with good will and ability, in enlightening the public on the subject. The question had been brought before them, and lie believed it was pretty well understood. He. would not therefore go over the same

ground again in making a formal statement of these Islands in n great measure, whether this what was contemplated in the establishment of the line, but would confine hims If to some points' left out in his former addresses, from inadvertence or any other cause, or not dwelt on with sufficient detail. Of modern inventions none has made such a rapid progress after its first discovery, as the Electric Telegraph. It is only a few years since the application of the Galvanic Battery to the purposes of a Telegraph Line was discovered, and the first Telegraph was constructed, and now it has spread over all parts of Europe, the United States and Canada, and is spreading still further into the less inhabited and civilized regions of the world. This fact of its rapid growth while yet in its infancy, is a sufficient indication of its value and importance. If it had not been an invention adapted to the wants of society in a greater degree than others, it would have, followed the same law of slow and gradual development. But it at Royal amongst the most useful and beneficial im- once shot up into maturity, and t ikes its place provements of the age. The Railway and the Telegraph are now introduced together in every country, in the East and the West, and are transforming the character of the world. Such a readiness to acknowledge its value and uses ns an agent of civilization, and unaniin its favor, has never been acceded to the practical application of any oth r of the discoveries of human j pay in addition whatever the work done in ex-

science. The project as you are aware is to unite the two continents of America by means ope- j of a Telegraph Line through the West Indies. For the union of the two continents of America, there are two directions of the L ne that might be taken, an Eastern and a Western Line. The latter would take its starting point from New Orleans and pass through Texas, Mexico, Central America, to the Isthmus, and from thence to the Republics of South America It would be a continental line, passing along terra firma, and might on that account be considered a more convenient line than the other, which passed through the chain of the West India Islands under the sea. But a little consideration will show that the former, the Western Line across the pathless forests and unhealthy swamps of the countries bordering on the Gulf of Mexico and the Carrtbean Sea, would be less secure and less easy of execution than the other line through the West Indies. It would take a longer time to come into operation ; and would he exposed to greater risk of injury from the uncivilized tribes of Indians through whose territories it would have to pass. A Telegraph requires to be protected from harm by the Government of the country ; in these countries there can be said to he a Government, any at rate one that would afford such security and certainty protection of as to justify the construc-

tion of a Telegraph. No doubt a line will pass in this direction, when the condition of these countries is changed, and a settled Government is established in them, and the people become more civilized ; but at present it would not be thought of seriously to lay a Telegraph Line through such a pathless wilderness as Yucatan or a country so disturbed as Nicaragua and even Mexico. Although a seeming paradox, the wires are safer when deposited on the bottom of the Atlantic than above the ground in countries not entirely civilized. The Eastern or Atlantic Mates are more settled and more advanced than the Southern and Western. The line through the West Indies would start from some point in Florida East, which will he placed in connection with the great cities of Baltimore, Philadelphia, and New York, and pass through the West India Islands, where it would find protection from a stable government ; and unite together a number of isolated but highly civilized communities. It appears then that in point of fact, at the present moment, this direction through the West Indies is the more favorable route, presenting less difficulties than the Western Line. It seems as if nature designed this chain of Islands for the connection of the two parts of the continent, separated from each other by the waters of the oceans on cither side. This chain formed by the Bahamas and the Lesser Antilles rise up in the sea like a barrier against the Atlantic, and a line of defence and communication from port to port,
within sight of each other from Florida to the Orinoque. It depends upon the inhabitants of

shall be the direction taken, whether the Teleshall graph shall pass to the direction take quite another East ; or whether it to the West. If it is not taken up by these Colonies, if they fail to accept the offer made to them and to promote the undertaking by their ready and liberal support and encouragement, you will force it into the other direction to the West. As to the difficulties of the undertaking they are not so considerable, as in the project of the Transatlantic Line, between England and America : which tvould not have obtained the confidence of capitalists, except through the wise liberality and foresight of the British Government, who agreed to furnish ships to take soundings, and to assist in the work of laying the cable, besides guaranteeing a yearly payment of £14,000. They are to have the use of the line to a certain extent for this payment. But suppose their Despatches in a year transmitted on the line only amounted to ,£5,000 Company they would still pay the same o£14 to 000 to the ; or if they amounted ,£10,000 they would still pay the ssune. But if the charge for the transmission of t lie Despatches exceeded this sum, and amounted to say, ,£16,000, then the Government agreed to pay the excess of <£2000, in addition to the yearly grant of .£14,000. Whether they used the Telegraph or not they it agreed to pay and in case they used beyond this extent, this sum, to

cess came to. This was liberal dealing, but yet it was a good bargain for all that. What did they get in return for their money 1 the transmission of 100 words every day from England to America, and of 100 words from America to England Now, this use of the Telegraph would scarcely suffice for the wants of the English Government in the daily correspondence between the Government and its Colonies in North America and the United States If the nature and extent of that intercourse is considered it will appear very probable that a much larger use of the Telegraph would be required. And when another line like the one now projected through the West Indies comes into operation it would add to the want. The English Government would therefore always have the full value of their annual grant to the Company in the use of the Line. I hey would also enjoy the privilege of priority for their Despatches þÿ and it. would he left to them to fix the tariff of charges for the transmission of messages. So that it was on the whole a very good bargain. Now, lie proposed to the Colonies a similar bargain, in some respect even more advantageous to them. He asked the Colonies to make a common payment of ,£7,000 for the support of the Line : in return for which they would have the use of it to a certain extent for the benefit of the pub-

lie : they should secure 2 per cent, of the capital in messages to be given to the public gratuitously : which is not proposed to be done in the Transatlantic line, and which constitutes a difference in favor of the liberality of the pro- j jected line in the West Indies. The contribu- j tion of 427,000 by the Colonies would be repaid by an equivalent amount of commercial and political information transmitted for the use of j the public, and for immediate publication. If the undertaking prospered the contribution would be reduced to £5,000, and still the same amount of information given. The projectors of the scheme might have addressed themselves to the British Government in the first instance but they thought it better to appeal to the Colonies, and see how they were disposed. And they began witlt Barbados because it was one of the most wealthy and important of them þÿ its inhabitants were noted for their intelligence, and their desire to adopt all the improvements so far as within their reach, and possessing a representative Government, where measures of public importance were freely canvassed, it appeared, that its example would have more weight and be more likely to influence public opinion in the other Colonies, in which the decision lies with a Council of Government. The course pursued in Barbados would very much contribute to the determination of the other Colonies, and to settle the question whether the Telegraph was to pass in this direction. They found in Bar-

Mr. Salles, arquebusier to the Emperor Napoleon, has invented a post-office automaton. which takes up every letter as it is thrown into the box, places it under the stamp, where it receives the postmark and date, and throws it out again for delivery to its destination. The process indicates the number of letters thus stamped. It is said that no less than 200 letters may be stamped by this machine in one minute. The General Post-office has made a trial of the invention, which has turned out satisfactory, and it is now in treaty with M. Salles for machines to be furnished to all the principal post-offices throughout France. The illegibility of postmarks, so often complained of, will, it is said, be completely obviated by the use of the automaton. þÿ London paper. ENGLISH HIGH LIFE The officers of the U. S. frigate Merrimac, lately at Southampton, have been entertained by Lord Hurdwicke. They say : þÿ Lord þÿHardwicke s family consists of his countess, his eldest sou ( about IS or 20, and Lord Royston by courtesy), three of the finest younger sons. The daughters Lady Elizabeth, looking daughters you ever þÿ saw, and several Lady Mary, and Lady Agnita þÿ are surpassingly beautiful : such development, such rosy checks, laughing eyes, and unaffected manners, you rarely see combined. They take a great deal of outdoor exercise, and came on hoard the 1 Merrimac in a heavy rain, with Irish thicker soled shoes than you or I ever wore, and cloaks and dresses almost impervious to wet. They steer their þÿfather yacht, s walk the Lord knows how mary miles, and þÿdon c t aro a cent about rain, besides doing a host of other things that would shock our ladies to death ; and yet in the parlor are the most elegant women in their satin shoes and diamonds I ever saw. þÿ After dinner, the ladies play and sing for us, and the other night they got up a game of þÿ þÿBlindtnan s þÿBuff, in which the ladies said we had the advantage, inasmuch as their þÿ petticoats rustled so that they were easily caught They call things by their names here. In the course of the game, Lord Hardwicke himself was blindfolded, and, trying to catch some one, fell over his þÿdaughter lap s on the floor, when two or three of the girls caught him by the legs and dragged his lordship, roaring with laughter, as we all

were, on his back into the middle of the floor. Yet they are perfectly respectful, but appear on a perfect equality with each other. In iact, the English are a great people. Two clubs here have offered us the use of their þÿrooms.

A TURKISH TWO-DECKER. The Fethirije, a Turkish two-decker, to carry 103 guns, has just been launebed. She is to go to England to be fitted with a crew. The ceremony was to have taken place at noon, and the corps diplomatique had received invitations to attend, the three-decker Mahmoudiek having been prepared for its reception. There was, however, some discrepancy between the opinions of the Sherefsaat, or astrologers, who are always consulted on such occasions, and the wishes of the Sultan, and the result was that the twodecker slipped off early in the morning, wounding ten men and ailing one or two, aud left nothing to see for the Sultan and his guests, who arrived at the hour appointed

These effusions were of course most amicable, and not a little sentimental, and they bore the impress (so at all events we are told) of being composed in those moments when the Royal heart is most expansive. Then again the Federal Government is annoyed that the hopes it held out to the Cantons are not yet realized ; the Cantons are indignant that they are not realized, and feel that they have been duped ; and poor Dr. Kern, conscious of having acted with much indiscretion, and of meriting the charge of overweening vanity, if not of more serious faults, is worried to death

by reproaches, to some of which he has certainly laid himself open. Russia has not named her Plenipotentiary ; until that is done no day can be fixed for the opening of the Conferences, and people here begin to suspect that there is an understanding on this point between Berlin and St. Petersburg. The King is also vexed that the Royalists should, before they were liberated, have signed a declaration that on their restoration to their country they would abide by the laws of the Canton of Neuchatel ; and, as might be expected, His Majesty profits by every circumstance to avoid fulfilling his promise, or what was entirely understood as a promise. The Emperor of the French is much to blame in this affair ; the moment the prisoners were liberated he should, without any delay, have summoned the King of Prussia to keep his word. He showed bad taste and no small ingratitude towards the Swiss in the beginning; the best way of redeeming his error was to have compelled his prevaricating þÿ broþÿther to perform his part of the implied bargain.

The Homoeopathic practice of treating diseases appears to be spreading in Barbados, as is shewn from the subjoined extract also taken from the West Indian : " To-night there is to he a Meeting of the friends of Homoeopathy, to bear a lecture

from Dr. Goding on the life of Hahneman, the founder of the system, it being the anniversary of his birth or death. Homoeopathy is spreading in Barbados, as is shewn by the fact of the complaints of the President of the Medical As sociation, that unless Legislative aid is afforded the members of tbe Profession, it is likely to die out with the present race of practitioners. Dr. Thomas proposes to give to each of them a stipend of -6300 a year out of the Public Treasury, besides the emoluments of their private practice. This wftuld he to deal with the Medical Profession even more liberally than with the Clerical or the legal ; but yet we do not mean to say, it is more liberal than they deserve, for no one disputes the value of their services, and but for the new fashion of Homoeopathy, they would no doubt be equally well rewarded. But here is a new theory of medicine to cure disease without medicine, that is, without taking nauseous drugs þÿ a theory that will always find ready acceptance. The strange thing is that this mode of treatment is found to answer quite as well as the other ; and it being infinitely the less disagreeable.

and the less expensive, it is no wonder it drives the other out of the field. Young men who are studying medicine with a view to practice it in Barbados would do well to make themselves acquainted with the Homoeopathic treatment as well as the regular practice, so as to be able to do what a really talented practitioner, (who has since got into a better field for the exertion f his dents in England) used to do, to practice both kinds þÿ large doses for those whose stomachs would still swallow them, and the infinitesimal doses for those who were more delicate, it is somewhat observable how many Barbadian physiciaus have subscribed to the Homoeopathic doctrines, and practice them with success j besides Dr. Goding, Dr. Sinckler, and Dr. Walcott here, there are Dr. Chapman (cousin of our Dr. Chapman, whose faith in the old system continues unshaken), Dr. Partridge, both of them in large practice in London ; Mr. Culpepper, who introduced Homoeopathy into Barbados and Mr. Trotman, residing in England. Dr. Sinckler and Dr. Walcott are also established in Homoeopathic practice in parts of þÿEngland. From the Londo n Times Correspondent Paris, March 31. A superior officer of Engineers of the Piedmontese army has arrived in Paris He is said to be charged by his Government with requesting the favour of being permitted to copy the old plans of the. fortifications of Alessandria, which were executed during the first Empire. It is the old French system which is to be followed at present. 1 alluded yesterday to the rumour of the probability of an arrangement, between the Vienna and Turin Cabinets through the good offices of France and England. Whether any temporary reconciliation will be patched up or not 1 cannot say, hut it is certain that so long as Austria and Piedmont stand in the position they do relatively to each other no sincere or durable friendship is possible between them. The crime of Sardinia is not that her press has now and then a strong article on Austrian politics, which is not allowed to penetrate into the Italian provinces of Austria ; the sin she has committed, still commits, and will, I trust, continue long to commit, and for which she can never hope for pardon from Vienna, is her free government, and the prosperity, beyond all comparison with the rest of the Italian Peninsula, which co-exists witli those liberties The Italian people cannot but contrast tlicir own situation with that of the subjects of Victor Emanuel ; and, however good the concessions recently granted to the Lombards, these will be ever turning a wistful eye to the country which

enjoys complete freedom. Under such circumstances no really good feeling can ever exist between them, and the restoration of diplomatic relations, which has been spoken of, will not diminish the dislike with which these Go vernments regard each other

HORRIBLE TORTIRE OF POLITICAL PRISONERS. sends the following: The Paris correspondent of the Morning Post þÿ " I have received a communication from Palermo, dated March 15, which is enough to make one hesitate and doubt whether we are not living in those days ofthe middle-age period, when human ingenuity was taxed to find out what amount of torture the body could suffer without expiring. You are already aware that torture has been practised in the prisons of Naples by the order of he King. But what is taking place in the island of Sicily iust now is still more horrible and revolting. There, by the order of his Christian Majesty Ferdinand II., King of the two Sicilies and Jerusalem, and the pious devotee of St. Gennaro, the prisons of Cefalu are turned into a holy political inquisition, accompanied by torture, executed by the newest mechanical invention of a human monster, who has been rewarded by his Sovereign for this diabolical contrivance with the order of Francesco Primo. The letter received contains a drawing of the instrument of torture, invented
by one Baiona, inspector of police, for the purpose of applying to all those who are supposed to be identified with the late revolt. It consists of a steel band, which passes over the

s f $ R Oj I AlV forehead and around the back of the head. This band is crossed by a second band of steel, which passes under the jaws, and is brought up to the crown of the head, where a screw is placed, which has the power of contracting the whole machinery. The author of this fiendish invention calls it ' La tortura del tSilcnzioi The object is to create such pain that, under a promise to speak, the victim, finding himself suddenly released, is supposed to be more likely to convey the desired intelligence. Such is the description given in a lengthy form by my correspondent, who goes 011 to siv : þÿ ' The first person who was tortured in the prisons of Cefalu is named Leo Ree. The instrument having been applied, the official set to watch him remained at his post until the victim, pallid, and with his eyes protuding, appeared to suffocate, and eventually showed no signs of life. He then left and called the higher authorities, including the doctor. The machine was removed, and the tortured man gradually showed signs of life, but was unable to utter a word. The guardian was flogged for calling the authorities too soon. One De Medici was the next victim, and then followed others I do not know. This system of torturing has revealed to the police a great number of the accomplices of Benterenga. Many persons, relatives and friends of the prisoners, have presented themselves to the authorities on hearing of what is taking place in the prisons, in order to save their friends from torture. In the prisons of

Cefalu there are more than 30 women subject to the most inhuman treatment. We at liberty are subject to every sort of injustice and cruelty. The other day the police, in order to find out Signor Civella, arrested his two brothers, his old uncle, a priest and a sister with a child at her breast. Civella is an exile, but it is thought that he may give him-elf up hearing from his friends what is taking p'ace. The brothers of Signor Botta have also been arrested to force him to surrender. Doctor has given himself up to save his sister, who, on his account, was seized in the country, and corded to a mule. Being enciente, she was delivered in this state prematurely. Doctor Guarneri has since been sent to the galleys. " The writer of this communication continues to add other heart-rending narratives. The students of Palermo are all ordered in doors after suufall, and the military are forbidden to speak to civilians. There is the greatest difficulty in conveying information from the island, as the utmost rigour is practised. The sailors, before embarking for Naples, are obliged to strip on shore in the presence of an inspector of police. A deadly and awful vengeance animates the whole population, and the writer anticipates again ' Sicilian vespers." Young girls, he says, are crying out for the blood of their oppressors. 'The King has personally ordered the torture to take place through his Lord Lieutenant, Prince Castelcieala, late Neapolitan Ambassador in London ' Such are the frightful details I this day received from
Palermo."

From the London Times.) THE PERSIAN WAR. Wo take tho following description of the brilliant affair under G moral Outr un near Bushire from tho Bombay 'Pe/egrap/i of March >, which reached us by the Overlaud Mail at a late hour this tuorniug. Further intelligence will be published in our Second Edition: þÿ " The Victoria, which arrived from the Gull on M mday afternoon, brought intelligence oi a rather smart engagement having been fought between the Biitish and Persian troops at a place called Kooshab on the 8th ult. Sir J .ones Outram, learning that a large body of Persians, under the command of Soojah-ool-Moolk in person, was hovering around Bushirc, resolved at once to briug matters to an issue 1 ue troops, consi-tiiig ofthe 3d Cavalry, the Poonah Horse, the 64th Foot, the 2J European Light lnlautry, the 78th Highlanders, the Sappers and Miners, the 20th Native Infant: y, tho 4th Rifles, the 26th Nativo Infantry, the Beloochers, 31 Troop Horse Artillery, 3d and 5th Light Field Batteries þÿ numbering in all 419 sabres, 2 212 European Infantry, 2,022 Native Infantry, and 18 guns, marched from Bushire on the evening ot the 3d of February. They were without tents or extra clothing of any sort; each man carried his greatcoat, blanket, and two days' cooked

provisions. After a march of 46 miles in 41 hours, during which they were exposed to the worst of weather, cold nights and deluging storms of rain, they readied the enemy's intrenched position oil the morning of the 5th, but found it abandoned. The enemy on hearing of our approach had evacuated their intrenobunmts so precipitately that their tents and camp equipage and ordnance magazine were abandoned ; the f rmer were being iapidly carried off by the ' vi ig pluml ovrs operating for some hours before we arrived. Every exertion was made to intercept there!: at of some bodies of the enemy's cavalry still in sight, and some little skirmishing with a tew horsemen took place, but eventually they all made off. After occupying for two days tho position the enemy had evacuated, and hearing that they had succeeded in getting the guns which they carried away into the difficult pass of Mliak, the troops commenced their return march 011 the night ofthe 7tb, carrying away the large stores ot flour, rice, and grain which the Persian Government had collected for their army, and destroying their magazine, found tocontaiu about 3.i,00jlb. of powder, with small-arm ammunition, and a vast quantity of shot and shell, thereby crippling the future operations of their army ; some of the guns arc supposed to have been cast into wells, and, as their wheels fell irto our hands, cannot again be used. At midnight an attack was made upon the rearguard by the enemy's horse, and parties threatened the Hue

of march on every side ; the troops were halted, and so formed as to protect the baggage aud resist the horsemen in whatever direction they might attempt to charge. Before this was quits completed four of the enemy's guns of heavy metal were opened upon the force, but the darkness of the night prevented any steps being taken to capture them. At break of day the Persian force, amounting to between 5,000 and <3,(100 men, witli five guns, was discovered on our left rear, north-east of our line of march The cavalry and artillery immediately moved rapidly to the attack, supported by two lines of infantry, a third protecting the baggage. The fire of artillery was most excellent and did groat execution, the cavalry also twice charged with great gallantry and success þÿ indeed, upon these two arms fell the whole brunt of the action, as the enemy moved away too rapidly for the infantry to overtake them. By 10 o'clock the defeat of the Persians was complete. Two guns were captured, the gun ammunition, laden upon mules, fell into our hands, and at least 700 men lay dead upon the field. The wounded, the number of whom must have been considerable, had been carried away, the remainder fled in a disorganiz d state, generally throwiug away their arms, which strewed the field in vast numbers, and nothing but, the paucity of our cavalry prevailed their total destruction and the capture of the remaining guns. The troops bivouacked for the d v eln«o to the battlefield, and at night cenmpli-l e l a march of 20 tni'es over a country

rendered almost impassable by the heavy rain which fell incessantly. After a rest of six hours the greater portion of the infantry continued their march to Bushire, which they reached before midnight on the 9th of February, thus performing another harassing march of 44 miles under incessant rain, besides fighting and defeating the enetny during its progress, within a short period of 50 hours. The cavalry and artillery, with an infantry escort, reached camp on the morning of the 10th ult. The result is most satisfactory, and will, Genl. Outram thinks, have a beneficial effect on our future operations in Persia

The quantity of sugar, cotton, and other tropical articles we are capable of producing was also discussed ; it may not, therefore, be irrelevant to make some remarks as to their quality. 1. To begin with our principal staple, Sugar, we are in a somewhat anomalous position. The sugar duties io England are so curiously arranged that for every improvement in quality extra duty is charged ; thus our Planters are actually obliged to manufacture their sugars of an inferior quality to get them into the home market at a lower duty. Without this preventive check it is hard to say, what state of perfection we might not otherwise have obtained ; indeed it is probable that by a first operation sugar could have been produced equal to the best refined þÿ as it is our sugars are considered both in the British and American markets about the best for refining purposes, and at the Paris Exhibition of 1855 the Hon. Control America. (From the Panama Star and Herald, April 2.) Costa Rita and the Central American War, The supporters of Walker in Nicaragua do riot hesitate, as a lust resort to help their failing cause, to assert that a large majority of the people d Costa Rica are anxious to join the stetr ranks, arid wait for an opportunity to revolt. A more base and unfounded libel was never uttered against a people than the foregoing; and the fact of the readiness and firmness with which they have kept tne field against their enemies is the best answer that can be given to the slander. In one paper we see it stated that General Mora had been taken prisoner ; in another that General

Canas was in favor of making terms with the enemy ; in a third that all Costa Rica is in favor of Walker. All these we know are incorrect, but t hey serve for the moment the purpose for which they are intended, namely, to induce ignorant adventurers to join Walker, under the belief that his government will soon be established. We believe from what we know of public feeling iu Costa Rica, that as long as she has a man left, she will contend against the filibustering band, who threaten her independence ; and whether she succeeds or is overpowered by superior numbers, the memory of the brave defence she has made for her liberty will form one of the brightest pages iu the annals of the history of Central America. Another malicious report set going by the invaders is, that Costa Rica makes war on United States citizens. She does nothing of the kind. Many citizens of that country live within her territory and enjoy all the liberties and privileges accorded to foreigners by the liberal laws of the country ; others are invited to corne and settle among the people, and their experience, their industry, and their intelligence is heartily welcomed by the government and the people. The people whom Costa Rica makes war on are those whose leader, in his " eternal enmity" celebrated proclamation, has declared against a people who have given them 110 cause of offence, and whose only crime is that they seek to preserve their independence and save thei homes from plunder and desolation.

In sending away the deserters from Walker's army, and paying all their expenses home, Costa Ricu lias sac an example of leniency and liberality which more advanced and more powerful nations may copy with advantage ; and we hope that the hundred and twenty-six men who returned to the United States by the Illinois will duly appreciate the kind treatment they received, and use all their influence to prevent others from falling into the snaie Walker had laid for them, and of running the risk of being indebted to thus against whom they took up arms, not only lor their lives but for the means of returning to their homes.

A Bold Preacher. þÿ The Paris correspondent of the Times writes on Monday: þÿ " Father Ventura continues his denunciations of Courtly vices in terms still more energetic than before. In his sermon of yesterday in the Chapel of the Tuilleries, and in the presence of the Emperor and the courtiers, his language was of the most unmistakable kind, and he spoke almost as it be had received the confessions of his auditory, and was authorized to declare them from the pulpit. He addressed himself directly to the Emperor ; he declared that, even if his life was moral and edifying, it was not sufficient if he did not stigmatize and drive from his presence all who might Scandalize the public by their vices, their corruption, or their profligacy. He said the Emperor was in error if he thought his private acts were confined to the walls of his Palace ; they were not ; he, and men like him, lived in a house of glass, and no secrets were safe from the prying eyes and the infidelity of courtiers. He told him that he was looked up to as a superior being, with powers for good or evil superior to all others, and that consequently more was expected from him. He denounced those who might sell the favour o- protection of the Court for gold, and who had grown rich in iniquity. In fact, the reverend father's language was so strong that persons by no means friendly to the Emperor thought he struck too hard in bis flagellation of magnificent sinners."
